gegangen wäre, indem er nicht bloss die Geschichte des peloponne-
sischen Krieges beendet, sondern noch die Erzählung der wich-
tigsten Ereignisse, welche während der folgenden vierzig Jahre
in Gri land dl hat. Dies würde aller-
dings hei anderweitiger Beglauhigung noch kein Beweis gegen die
Richtigkeit jener Annahme sein, denn man könnte glauben, dass
Xenophon ursprünglich mit dem Ende des peloponnesischen Krieges
ahgeschlossen und erst später, ohne auf seinen früheren Plan
Rücksicht zu nehmen, die Aufzeichnung der nachfolgenden Begeben-
heiten angefügt hahe, so dass wir gewissermassen zwei gelrennte
Werke vor uns hätten. Und in der That lässt sich am Ende des
zweiten Buches ein solcher Ahschluss nicht verkennen, aber auch
dieser greift üher den peloponnesischen Krieg hinaus, der schon
mit dem zweiten Kapitel dieses Buches zu Ende geführt war.
Auch würde gewiss Xenophon jenen Plan, wenn auch nur mit
wenigen Worten, angedeutet, und nicht seinem Werke den sonder-
baren Anfang μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα gegehen hahen. Dass aber Xenophon
heahsichtigt habe, des Thukydides Werk und sein eigenes ge-
i als ein Ganzes ll und dass deswegen die
Erzählung ohne die geringste Andeutung fortfahre, wo die des
Thukydides ahbricht, darf man nicht voraussetzen; d

1. 26. οὐ συμπεφυκὼς δεδήσομαι: "1 shall not be bound to him for

the continuance of an action, or the permanence of its results, in future

Ll 27. τὴν λείαν; ‘the cattle of the enemy they drove off as booty.’
We have here an carly and curious attempt to define the degree of pro-
tection which may be accorded to private property in time of war, The
principle seems to be that property which could not be removed, as, for
instance, standing corn, should be respected: but that all which could,
as, for instance, herds of cattle, should be fair prize if the owners were
so careless as to Jet it be taken. In this desire ὅτι μικρότατον τοῦ πολέμου
λιπεῖν. to confine the sufferings entailed by war within as narrow limits as
possible, Xenophon shows a humanity worthy of the disciple of Socrates,
but many centuries in advance of his age.

1. 23. τοῖς ἐπὶ μακρὸν πορευομένοις : ‘those who are marching in a
long column must be at a long distance from their supports.” Here
again Xenophon is imparting to his readers a lesson in strategy drawn
from the rich stores of his personal experience. In marching past a
fortified post two rules are to be observed : (1) the distance of the line ot
march from the walls must not be less than the length of the column.
Otherwise, supposing the column to be attacked at either extremity, those
at the other extremity will have farther to go to strengthen the point
threatened, than the enemy to assault it; (2) in drawing off, the rear
must be gradually strengthened, so that the part of the column opposite
to the gate of the town may always be the strongest.

I. τό. τοσοῦτοι γὰρ ἦσαν οἱ ταξίαρχοι: the division of the
Persian contingent was probably, according to Xenophon's idea,
as follows. It consisted originally of 31000 men (1 v 5). These
were divided into μυριοστύας, χιλιοστύας, τάξεις, λόχους, δεκάδας
and πεμπάδας under the respective command of μυρίαρχοι,
χιλίαρχοι, ταξίαρχοι, λοχαγοί, δεκάδαρχοι and πεμπάδαρχοι.
These two latter are sometimes spoken of as δωδεκάδαρχοι (or
δωδέκαρχοι 11 iv 4) and ἐξάδαρχοι. A πέμπας consisted of five
soldiers and one officer, who was called πεμπάδαρχος or éfd-
dapyos, according as he was excluded from or included in the
reckoning. Two πεμπάδες constituted a δεκάς, i.e. 10 common
soldiers and two πεμπάδαρχοι, one of whom, however, com-

πλῆθος, ad quod conciliandum Cyrus ἐν τῷ φανερῷ ἑαυτὸν παρέχειν
debuerat): ei contrarii sunt ἄλλοι qui eum domi suae convenirent ;
ut par esset dignas ei aedes contingere...Videtur autem vicinum
τρόπου fefellisse librarium, Idem legisse videtur Gabrielius qui
reddit nunc autem quando non id solum consecutus es sed potes
etiam alios, quos tibi commodum sit, conciliare et adiungere; Mad-
vigius νῦν δ᾽ ἐπεὶ οὐ τρόπῳ μόνῳ ἂν ἔχεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλοις
ἀνακτᾶσθαι δύνασαι ols καιρός, εἴη ἂν ἥδη.. ἄξιον (neque enim
agi de aliis conciliandis sed de iis, quos placuerit, et moribus et
aliis rebus conciliandis); Hertleinius νῦν δ᾽ ἐπεὶ οὐχ οὕτω μόνον
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλως ἀνακτᾶσθαι δύνασαι (omisso τρόπον et ἔχεις
codicum : Hermannus autem ἄλλως iam coniecerat, teste Bor-
nemanno). Hugius denique quam proxime vestigia premens CD
codicum scripsit οὐ τούτῳ τῷ τρόπῳ μόνον ἄρχεις, adnotans:
"οὗτος ὁ τρόπος est mos usque ad hoc tempus observatus, mos τοῦ
συμπονεῖν, τοῦ συγκινδυνεύειν, τοῦ ἐν φανερῷ εἶναι, Iam
amplo imperio potitus poterit Cyrus in eo exercendo etiam vim
adhibere vel minas, poterit porro homines conciliare magnificentia,
luxuria, donis opulentis, conviviis lautis: ‘er ist nicht mehr auf
jene elementaren Mittel angewiesen’ ut dicunt nostrates’. Cf. vin
ii 2. 1. 325. pro οὗ Hartmanus legendum esse
censet ἧς, expulso v. χωρίον.

and style as altogether in disagreement with both. Thus—to
take only two points—Xenophon has a symmetrical way of pre-
senting what he has to tell, and the narrative that begins with
Cyrus’ childish sallies ends fitly with his death-bed speech : the
Epilogue, ignoring Cyrus’ prominence as hero throughout, takes us
tediously back through the Persian institutions which were the
outcome of his life, merely to contrast them as institutions with
those of the writer's own day. Xenophon, even when treating
at some length on one main subject (6.9. Cyrus’ popularity, in
